Face-to-face (public venue or private visit) OR digital (video recorded at a time and place of the candidate's choice, with no fixed sessions; video uploaded at booking or within 28 days). Performance only: 30-minute programme (±2 min), timed from the first note to the last. Marks: pieces 30 (60%) + performance as a whole 20 (40%) = 50. Distinction 45–50, Merit 40–44, Pass 34–39, Below Pass 17–33.

At least 20 minutes from the ARSM repertoire list for the instrument, plus up to 10 minutes of own-choice music at Grade 8 standard or above. No written or spoken elements and no other tests (no viva, no programme notes, no quick study). Candidates submit a programme form, or enter programme details online for digital exams.
sections: About the repertoire list

Official ARSM repertoire list for double bass, read from the ABRSM PDF (17 entries). Candidates may choose to play any of the works using editions published for either solo scordatura or orchestral tuning, provided the piano part is suitably transposed wherever necessary. Own-choice music is also allowed within the programme rules above. Check the board's current list before entering; lists are updated online.
General notes

Pathway as of Oct 2026: ARSM (L4) → LRSM (L6) → FRSM (L7). DipABRSM is withdrawn (last date 31 Dec 2023). The old-format LRSM closed 30 Apr 2024 and the old FRSM closed 31 Oct 2024. All three current diplomas require only Grade 8 in the instrument (ABRSM or an equivalent board for LRSM/FRSM). No Grade 5 or 6 theory prerequisite is stated for any current performance diploma. Under the old syllabus, Grade 5 theory appeared only as a condition on some substitutions. ARSM has no written element. LRSM/FRSM need a written (2,000 / 3,500 words) or spoken-video (10 / 17 min) supporting-evidence submission. Digital exams have no fixed sessions: book, pay and upload any time; for digital ARSM the video goes in at booking or within 28 days. Specific LRSM/FRSM upload windows weren't stated in the spec, which refers to abrsm.org/how-to-book. ABRSM discontinued printed diploma syllabuses, and lists are updated online, so re-check the abrsm.org pages before entering. abrsm.org HTML pages returned redirect errors to the fetch tool, so some details come from the PDFs and ABRSM's Taiwan mirror.
General rules (all instruments)

Both LRSM and FRSM programmes must be balanced and varied: a variety of moods, keys and tempi and at least two pieces or movements contrasting by period or style. Works and movements must be played complete unless the repertoire list says otherwise, and any list-specific instructions must be followed. Music published with an accompaniment must be performed with one; any suitable instrument may accompany provided the candidate stays the main soloist, candidates arrange their own accompanist, and pre-recorded accompaniments are not allowed unless the composer intended them. Memory is not required (but encouraged if it helps). Any edition matching the list entry may be used and own-choice music must exist as a legible, fully notated score; performing from unauthorised photocopies of copyright editions is not allowed. Own-choice may include the candidate's own composition or arrangement but must still be at or above the required standard, and ABRSM cannot give prior approval of own-choice standard. An audience is encouraged but not required. Infringements (wrong length, too much own choice without approval, wrong movements, edited video) can bring a warning, mark deduction or disqualification. A video can only ever be submitted once, and the same Unit 2 work cannot be reused at a higher level.

Official FRSM repertoire list for double bass, read from the ABRSM PDF (36 entries). Candidates may choose to play any of the works using editions published for either solo scordatura or orchestral tuning, provided the accompaniment is suitably transposed wherever necessary. Own-choice music is also allowed within the programme rules above. Check the board's current list before entering; lists are updated online.
General notes

Pathway as of Oct 2026: ARSM (L4) → LRSM (L6) → FRSM (L7). DipABRSM is withdrawn (last date 31 Dec 2023). The old-format LRSM closed 30 Apr 2024 and the old FRSM closed 31 Oct 2024. All three current diplomas require only Grade 8 in the instrument (ABRSM or an equivalent board for LRSM/FRSM). No Grade 5 or 6 theory prerequisite is stated for any current performance diploma. Under the old syllabus, Grade 5 theory appeared only as a condition on some substitutions. ARSM has no written element. LRSM/FRSM need a written (2,000 / 3,500 words) or spoken-video (10 / 17 min) supporting-evidence submission. Digital exams have no fixed sessions: book, pay and upload any time; for digital ARSM the video goes in at booking or within 28 days. Specific LRSM/FRSM upload windows weren't stated in the spec, which refers to abrsm.org/how-to-book. ABRSM discontinued printed diploma syllabuses, and lists are updated online, so re-check the abrsm.org pages before entering. abrsm.org HTML pages returned redirect errors to the fetch tool, so some details come from the PDFs and ABRSM's Taiwan mirror.
General rules (all instruments)

Both LRSM and FRSM programmes must be balanced and varied: a variety of moods, keys and tempi and at least two pieces or movements contrasting by period or style. Works and movements must be played complete unless the repertoire list says otherwise, and any list-specific instructions must be followed. Music published with an accompaniment must be performed with one; any suitable instrument may accompany provided the candidate stays the main soloist, candidates arrange their own accompanist, and pre-recorded accompaniments are not allowed unless the composer intended them. Memory is not required (but encouraged if it helps). Any edition matching the list entry may be used and own-choice music must exist as a legible, fully notated score; performing from unauthorised photocopies of copyright editions is not allowed. Own-choice may include the candidate's own composition or arrangement but must still be at or above the required standard, and ABRSM cannot give prior approval of own-choice standard. An audience is encouraged but not required. Infringements (wrong length, too much own choice without approval, wrong movements, edited video) can bring a warning, mark deduction or disqualification. A video can only ever be submitted once, and the same Unit 2 work cannot be reused at a higher level.
Other components

Unit 2 is a written submission (3500 words, plus or minus 10%, PDF) or a spoken video presentation (17 minutes, plus or minus 10%) on one of four options: Informing your audience, Detailed analysis, Programming your performance, or Preparation for performance, based on substantial personal research and reflection. Same format, translation/subtitle and declaration rules as LRSM. First page of each own-choice piece is uploaded as PDF.

General notes

No Grade 8 or Theory of Music prerequisite for any performance diploma (Trinity entry-requirements page and March 2026 syllabus). Current documents: 'Classical Music Performance Diplomas' syllabus, online edition March 2026 (resource id 8556, same for all instruments; Trinity points to trinitycollege.com/performance-diplomas for the current version) and 2026-edition instrument repertoire lists. Digital diplomas (ATCL, LTCL) allow recorded/backing-track accompaniment; face-to-face exams need a live accompanist. Own-choice programme approval: whole programme only, usually within 15 working days; the syllabus says the approval letter is valid 3 years, while a support article says 2 years (conflict, check the letter). Works on any current Trinity grade, certificate or lower-diploma list cannot be own-choice, and a work approved for one diploma cannot be reused at a higher diploma. General rules (all instruments)

Applies to all instruments. Performance times cover all works including short breaks between movements (about 10 seconds maximum) but not between works; the minimum has no leeway and under-length recitals are referred and penalised, while over-length ones may be curtailed. Programmes show a range of moods, styles and tempi. Use only one instrument type (family members such as flute and piccolo allowed; for flute at most one piece on piccolo or alto flute). Unaccompanied works may make up to 40% of an accompanied programme (one long listed work above 40% is accepted); pieces published with accompaniment may not be played unaccompanied; the candidate provides one accompanist (normally). Repeats: observe da capo and dal segno but do not play exposition or recapitulation repeats, repeats of more than two bars, or repeats within variations (Baroque suite repeats are allowed only if musically justified by ornamentation). Long introductions, endings and tuttis must be shortened (up to 30 seconds allowed). All cadenzas should be played. Memory is not required and earns no marks; metronomes and spoken introductions are not allowed. Music must be from a reliable, unaltered edition and legal copies are needed (copies for the examiner, and originals shown). Stagecraft is marked. A written programme (names, date, composers, full titles with movements and opus numbers, timing per piece and total, in order) is required.
Other components

Programme and planning section: a written programme (2 marks) and planning, balance and construction of the programme (2 marks). No viva, quick study or written submission; detailed notes are not required at ATCL.

lists: Prelude and any other two movts

p0462.d: Hindemith's flute sonata (1936): a cheerful, neoclassical first movement, a grave slow movement, and a lively finale ending in a march. Clear-cut, contrapuntal and rhythmically crisp.

s0002.d: La Captive, the first of Beach's Op. 40 pieces, arranged for double bass. A brooding, song-like melody that needs a singing tone and secure intonation high on the instrument.
s0002.rw: Rare Romantic lyrical piece for bass

s0007.d: Arrangement of Arthur Benjamin's popular Jamaican Rumba. Bouncy Caribbean syncopation; practises rhythmic precision and a light, crisp bow.
s0007.rw: Fun, catchy rhythm piece; a student favourite

s0011.d: A playful, quick character piece for double bass. Practises nimble fingers and crisp, lightly detached bowing.

s0014.d: A humorous, quirky bass character piece with sudden contrasts. Practises articulation, rhythmic bite and agile bowing.

s0018.d: Arrangement of the elegant Gavotte from Ambroise Thomas's opera Mignon. Graceful and witty, practising neat staccato and phrasing.

s0028.d: A very simple arrangement of the spiritual All Night, All Day (Angels Watching Over Me). Gentle lullaby-like tune practising open strings and steady bowing.

s0032.d: A short tango for double bass with characteristic accents and rhythm. Practises rhythmic precision and a strong bow.

s0034.d: A spooky, playful bass dance in a minor key. Practises rhythm and characterful articulation.

s0042.d: Arrangement of the title song from Disney's Beauty and the Beast (Menken & Ashman). Gentle, lyrical melody; can be played as a duet.

s0051.d: A short tune from Essential Elements Book 1 for beginners. Practises simple rhythm and open strings.

s0053.d: A stately, Renaissance-style pavane for Initial grade, used across all four string instruments. Practises slow, even bowing.

s0055.d: A playful piece for double bass with a dance character. Practises rhythmic precision and articulation.

s0068.d: Arrangement of the Christmas song Jolly Old St Nicholas for beginner bass. Practises simple rhythm.

s0076.d: The aria Tre giorni son che Nina, once attributed to Pergolesi, arranged for double bass. A tender, lyrical melody that needs a singing tone and long phrases.

s0079.d: Arrangement of a German folk tune (likely the one known in English as The More We Get Together). Simple and cheerful, for early bass players.

s0081.d: An 18th-century vocal solfeggio (exercise) by Aprile, arranged for bass (ornaments optional). Lyrical and graceful.

s0100.d: Arrangement of Harold Arlen's march-like song from The Wizard of Oz (1939); a cheerful, bouncy tune that practises steady rhythm and clean string crossings. Double bass version from Abracadabra.
s0100.rw: Fun, familiar tune for young bassists

s0103.d: Arrangement of Harold Arlen's march-like song from The Wizard of Oz (1939); a cheerful, bouncy tune that practises steady rhythm and clean string crossings. Abracadabra double bass version, playable as a duet or with piano.
s0103.rw: Familiar tune; duet option is appealing

s0105.d: A substantial 20th-century double bass solo by the American composer Armand Russell, built as variations over a repeating chaconne pattern. Demands range, varied bow strokes and sustained concentration.
s0105.rw: Serious, idiomatic bass writing; demanding to sustain

s0108.d: Opening pair from an 18th-century sonata attributed to the cellist 'Giovannino', played on double bass: a solemn Adagio then a crisp staccato Aria. Practises tone in slow playing and clear articulation.

s0109.d: Lively first movement of a sonata in F attributed to Giovannino, adapted for double bass. Busy Baroque figuration that demands good intonation and agile bowing in the upper register.
s0109.rw: Good Baroque workout; standard bass repertoire

s0110.d: Third movement of the Giovannino Sonata in A minor for double bass, contrasting detached and singing (arioso) material. Tests changes of bow style and phrasing.
s0110.rw: Useful contrast piece for bow control

s0111.d: The well-known 'Eccles' Sonata in G minor in a double bass transcription: a grave, expressive Adagio and an energetic Corrente. A cornerstone of the advanced bass repertoire.
s0111.rw: Classic bass repertoire; rewarding and well loved

s0113.d: Arrangement of the Tudor song 'Pastime with good company', attributed to Henry VIII. A sturdy, dance-like tune that practises firm rhythm and confident bowing.

s0116.d: Arrangement for double bass of the D minor minuet from the Anna Magdalena Bach Notebook. A short, graceful dance practising even rhythm and smooth bowing.

s0117.d: Arrangement of a minuet from the Anna Magdalena Bach Notebook, transposed to C for double bass. A well-known, gentle Baroque dance focusing on clean intonation and phrasing.

s0118.d: The famous 'Paradis' Sicilienne (now thought to be by Samuel Dushkin) arranged for double bass. A gentle, lilting melody in 6/8 that tests sustained tone and expressive control high on the instrument.
s0118.rw: Beautiful melody; lets bassists show tone

s0128.d: Opening pair from Marcello's A minor sonata, played on double bass: a grave, expressive Adagio and a vigorous Allegro. Classic bass repertoire demanding tone and agility.

s0129.d: First two movements of Marcello's G major cello sonata: a lyrical, ornamented Adagio and a lively, buoyant Allegro. Straightforward Baroque style good for tone and articulation.

s0135.d: Two movements from Marcello's F major sonata, arranged for double bass: a broad, singing Largo and a bright Allegro.

s0158.d: A Bach Gavotte in G minor in this arrangement: a stately, dance-like Baroque piece needing clear rhythm and good intonation in higher positions.

s0173.d: A simple Bach-based piece from an Essential String Method book, arranged by Nelson for beginners. Likely a call-and-response style melody practising basic bowing and pulse.

s0183.d: Double bass arrangement of the D minor Polonaise from the Anna Magdalena Bach Notebook. A stately, dignified dance practising rhythm and phrasing.

s0189.d: Double bass arrangement of a mazurka by Natalia Baklanova. A lively Polish-style dance in triple time with accented beats.

s0970.d: A brisk, cheerful Baroque bourrée in duple time with steady crotchet-quaver drive; good for clean shifting and even bow strokes on the bass.
s0970.rw: Solid Baroque dance; tidy and well paced

s0971.d: A simple, poised arrangement of a Handel gavotte with its characteristic half-bar upbeat; practises clear phrasing and light, detached bowing.

s0992.d: A Handel Allegro arranged for double bass; brisk Baroque movement working steady rhythm, shifting and clear articulation.

s1005.d: A short tutor-book piece from Double Bass Basics; a simple, characterful tune practising basic bowing and first finger patterns.

s1010.d: Arrangement of a German-style dance by the Renaissance composer Valentin Haussmann; sturdy, simple dance rhythms in early positions.

s1011.d: A gentle, slightly wistful waltz by the Finnish bassist Teppo Hauta-aho; lyrical melody in triple time that shows off the bass's singing upper register.
s1011.rw: Idiomatic bass writing by a bass specialist

s1012.d: Opening movement of Hauta-aho's unaccompanied Jazz Sonatine No. 2; swung rhythms and walking-bass ideas for solo bass.
s1012.rw: Fun jazz idiom; idiomatic for bass

s1013.d: Third movement of Hauta-aho's unaccompanied Jazz Sonatine No. 2; jazzy, rhythmically lively solo writing.
